One powerful machine is split by a hypervisor into several independent virtual servers, and each one behaves like a dedicated computer: its own operating system, its own users, its own IP address, and a guaranteed share of CPU, RAM and disk.
32	
33	## How virtualization works
34	
35	The host machine runs a **hypervisor** (KVM is the industry standard, and what Nxeon uses). The hypervisor carves the hardware into virtual machines. Each VM thinks it owns real hardware — it boots its own Linux kernel, mounts its own disk, and can be rebooted or reinstalled without touching its neighbors.

40	
41	On a VPS you get the **root** account, the system administrator. That means you can:
42	
43	- Install any software: databases, language runtimes, Docker, custom binaries.
44	- Open and close network ports and configure your own firewall.
45	- Tune the kernel, mount extra storage, or run background services.
46	- Reinstall the whole operating system whenever you want.
47	
48	Shared hosting hides all of this behind a control panel. A VPS hands you the keys.
49	
50	## A quick anatomy
51	
52	When you order a VPS you'll pick a few things:
53	
54	- **vCPU** — virtual processor cores. More cores means better handling of concurrent work.
55	- **RAM** — working memory. This is usually the first thing you run out of.
56	- **NVMe storage** — fast solid-state disk. NVMe drives are many times faster than the SATA SSDs older hosts still use, which makes databases and file operations snappy.
57	- **Bandwidth** — how much data you can transfer each month.
58	- **An operating system image** — Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, Rocky and so on.
59	
60	## When is a VPS the right choice?
61	
62	A VPS is the sweet spot for anyone who has outgrown shared hosting but does not need a whole physical server. Common uses:
63	
64	- Hosting one or many websites with full control over the stack.
65	- Running a web app (Node.js, Python, PHP, Go) with its own database.
66	- Self-hosting tools like Nextcloud, a Git server, or a VPN.
67	- Development and staging environments.
68	- Bots, scrapers, cron jobs, and background workers.
69

71	
72	- **Shared hosting** — cheapest, but you share everything and get no root. Fine for a small brochure site.
73	- **VPS** — private, root access, guaranteed resources, great price-to-power ratio.

101	    body: `Every hosting company sells the same four broad tiers under a hundred marketing names. Once you understand what actually separates them, choosing is easy.
102	
103	## Shared hosting
104	
105	Hundreds of websites live on one server and share its CPU, memory and disk. A control panel manages everything for you; you never see a command line.
106	
107	- **Pros:** cheapest option, zero server management.
108	- **Cons:** no root access, no guaranteed resources, and a "noisy neighbor" spike can slow your site. You can only run what the host allows.
109	- **Best for:** a small blog or brochure site with modest traffic.
110	
111	## VPS hosting
112	
113	A physical server is split by a hypervisor into isolated virtual servers. Each gets **guaranteed** CPU, RAM and NVMe storage plus **full root access**.
114	
115	- **Pros:** private and predictable performance, install anything, your own firewall and OS, excellent price-to-power ratio.

120

122	
123	- **Pros:** maximum raw performance and total control of the hardware.

125	- **Best for:** very high traffic, heavy databases, or strict compliance needs.

128	
129	Cloud is really a *delivery model* for VPS-style instances: you spin them up in seconds, resize on the fly, and often pay by the hour. Underneath, each instance is a virtual server much like a VPS.
130

153	
154	For most people the honest answer is a VPS. It's the tier that gives you real control and guaranteed performance without dedicated-server pricing.

182	## RAM is usually the first wall you hit
183	
184	Memory is where most projects run short. Every process — your web server, database, language runtime, control panel — holds RAM. Run out and Linux starts killing processes (the dreaded OOM killer) or thrashing swap, and everything crawls.
185	
186	Rough starting points:
187	
188	- **1 GB** — a small static site, a single lightweight service, a bot.
189	- **2 GB** — a WordPress site, a small Node.js app, a personal Nextcloud.

- **Registry Expiry Date** — when the registration lapses if not renewed. This is the field to watch if you're hoping to catch a dropping domain, or making sure your own doesn't expire.

A port check has three possible results, and knowing the difference saves hours:

- **Open** — something is listening and accepting connections. Good.

- **Filtered** — a firewall is silently dropping your packets, so you get no answer at all (the connection "times out"). This is the most confusing case because the service may be running fine behind the firewall.

\`\`\`

\`\`\`

example.com.    AAAA    2001:db8::10

    publishedAt: new Date("2026-07-05"),
    body: `\`Connection refused\` is one of the most common — and most misdiagnosed — errors in networking. People assume it's a firewall, spend an hour on firewall rules, and never fix it, because the error is actually telling them something quite specific. Understand what it means and the fix usually takes minutes.

## What "connection refused" really means

Here's the crucial distinction:

- **Connection refused** means your packet *reached the server*, but **nothing was listening** on that port. The operating system actively sent back a rejection (a TCP RST). You got an answer — a "no."
- **Connection timed out** means your packet **got no answer at all**, usually because a firewall silently dropped it, or the host is unreachable. You got silence.

This difference is your biggest clue. **Refused = reached the machine, no service there. Timeout = something is blocking the path.** If you're seeing "refused," a network firewall is usually *not* your problem — the packet clearly got through.

## The usual causes of "connection refused"

1. **The service isn't running.** The most common cause by far. Nothing is listening, so the OS refuses.
2. **The service is listening on the wrong address.** It's bound to \`127.0.0.1\` (localhost only) but you're connecting from outside. Local works, remote is refused.
3. **The service is on a different port** than you're connecting to.
4. **The service crashed or failed to start** and you didn't notice.

## Step-by-step diagnosis

Work from the service outward — this order finds it fastest.

**Step 1: Is the service even running?**

\`\`\`
sudo systemctl status nginx
\`\`\`

If it's \`inactive\` or \`failed\`, that's your answer. Start it and read the logs if it won't stay up:

\`\`\`
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo journalctl -u nginx --no-pager -n 50
\`\`\`

**Step 2: Is anything listening on the port?**

\`\`\`
sudo ss -tulpn | grep :443
\`\`\`

No output means nothing is bound to that port — the service isn't listening where you think.

**Step 3: What address is it bound to?**

This is the sneaky one. Look at the local address in the \`ss\` output:

- \`127.0.0.1:5432\` — **localhost only.** Remote connections will be refused. Databases ship like this by default.
- \`0.0.0.0:443\` or \`*:443\` — listening on **all interfaces.** Reachable externally.

## MX records: where incoming mail goes

An **MX (Mail Exchange)** record tells the world which servers accept email for your domain. When someone emails \`you@example.com\`, their server looks up the MX records for \`example.com\` and delivers there.

\`\`\`
example.com.    MX    10    mail.example.com.

\`\`\`

- MX records point to a **hostname, not an IP**, and that hostname needs its own A record. You also can't point an MX at a CNAME — use a real hostname.

Your MX records are completely independent of your website's A record, which is why you can host your site on your VPS and your email with a provider like Google Workspace or Fastmail at the same time.

Receiving your mail is one thing; getting *your outbound* mail trusted is another. Spammers forge sender addresses constantly, so mailbox providers won't trust a domain that hasn't proven which servers may send for it. Three TXT-based records do that proving.

\`\`\`
example.com.    TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:mail.example.com ~all"
\`\`\`

\`\`\`
